To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
semantic information can influence attention even when the semantic relationships are task irrelevant and when more predictive cues are available.
Semantic information biases attention even when it is irrelevant to the task.
the semantic properties of an object influence attentional allocation, even if these properties are irrelevant to a task.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of semantic information in visual attention.
the influence of irrelevant semantic information on visual selection and demonstrates the importance of semantic properties for attention.
the influence that semantic information exerts on the visual system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the semantic information is always processed, even when the task does not require it.
semantic information biases attentional allocation when it is relevant for the ongoing task and even when it is not.
semantic information is a source of attentional bias that is independent of the ongoing task and that is contingent on the attended object.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
semantic information exerts an attentional bias on visual attention even if it is not task relevant.
the semantic bias on attention is a general phenomenon, and it is not limited to situations in which the semantic information is necessary for the task.
semantic properties bias visual attention in a similar way as low-level properties.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the semantic bias may represent a default mode of operation, which is modulated by attentional control.
semantic properties of objects are a source of bias on attentional selection even when they are irrelevant.
semantic information is always present in the environment and that it influences visual attention even when it is not necessary for the task.
